correctness.rationale: Cut energy cannot decrease under closed-neighborhood minority updates; a strict increase is available, possibly after one neutral flip, whenever a cross matching edge is uncut in balanced cliques. Balancing overfull cliques is always legal. The proof constructs a finite positive-probability route to a maximum cut from every state, ruling out other terminal components. For even n every maximum cut is absorbing; for odd n matched bits freeze and unmatched bits move by reversible adjacent-rank subset exchanges; each product of rank-inclusion graphs is connected with uniform invariant law. Binomial formulas follow from ranks and the bijection adding two unmatched vertices establishes R_(2k+1,t)=R_(2k+2,t) for t≤2k+1. A separate direct transition-graph construction and terminal strongly connected component calculation matched all 18 instances n=2..5 and all t; targeted n=6,t=2 gave 104 singleton absorbing states, matching the four odd classes (16,36,36,16). The graph tests are finite corroboration only.
residual_risks: Only two equal n-cliques with disjoint unweighted cross matching, sequential closed-neighborhood minority and tie-retention.

originality.rationale: Rouquier–Regnault–Thierry (2011), Theorem 4.1, already supplies the stochastic minority rule, energy monotonicity and isolated clique attractors. It does not analyze two equal cliques joined by an arbitrary disjoint matching or their recurrent-class vector and parity-preserving total count. Related clique bouquets share a hub; matching-deleted bicliques have a different interaction graph. Those named findings do not dominate this two-clique matching interpolation. Best-of-knowledge originality remains conditional on unindexed bridged-clique studies.
residual_risks: A broader theorem for stochastic minority on two-community graphs might contain this matching family without matching terminology.
A finite SCC calculation verifies bounded n but the all-n transience proof requires the constructive strict-improvement argument.
